explain.title: Elements can have different formula forms
explain.body: Some elements are represented by their symbols alone, such as Na, Ca, C and Fe. Other elements exist as molecules, such as O₂, N₂ and H₂. O₃ is ozone: each molecule contains three oxygen atoms.

explain.title: Ionic compounds use formula units
explain.body: In an ionic solid such as sodium chloride, oppositely charged ions form a crystal. Its formula unit shows the minimum ratio of the ions. NaCl has a 1:1 ratio; CaCl₂ has a 1:2 ratio of calcium to chlorine.

explain.title: Covalent compounds have molecular formulae
explain.body: Covalent compounds generally exist as molecules. The textbook defines a molecular formula this way: “A chemical compound is thus, represented by a chemical formula which is called the molecular formula of that compound and which shows all the types of atoms bonded together in one molecule of that compound.” For example, H₂O shows two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom in one molecule.

explain.title: Read subscripts carefully
explain.body: A small number after a symbol tells you how many of that atom are present. No subscript means one. In NH₃ there is one nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms.

explain.title: Formula and structure are not always the same thing
explain.body: A formula can show the simplest ratio in an ionic or extended solid without meaning that separate molecules exist. For example, SiO₂ represents the 1:2 ratio of silicon to oxygen in sand’s structure.

mistakes: Treating an ionic formula unit as if it described a separate molecule.
Forgetting that an element can exist as a molecule, such as O₂, rather than as single atoms.
Reading a missing subscript as zero; no subscript means one atom.
Changing a polyatomic ion’s subscripts instead of putting brackets around the ion, for example writing NH₄₂CO₃ instead of (NH₄)₂CO₃.
Writing a formula with charges that do not balance, or not reducing the ion ratio to the simplest whole numbers.
Assuming that every different compound must have a different molecular formula; structural isomers can share one.

explain.body: Empirical Formula of a compound shows the simplest whole number ratio of atoms present in that compound.

explain.title: Ionic compounds
explain.body: All the ionic compounds are represented by their empirical formulas. These formulas show the simplest ratio present between their ions. Calcium fluoride, CaF₂, shows the ratio present between calcium and fluoride ions in its crystal.

explain.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
explain.body: For covalent chemical compounds, which exist as molecules, the empirical formulas may be different from their molecular formulas. Hydrogen peroxide is H₂O₂ and its empirical formula is HO; benzene is C₆H₆ and its empirical formula is CH.

explain.title: Same empirical formula
explain.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest ratio, not the actual number of atoms. Benzene (C₆H₆) and acetylene (C₂H₂) both have the empirical formula CH. Water's molecular and empirical formulas are both H₂O.

mistakes: Copying the molecular formula as the empirical formula without checking whether all the subscripts can be divided by the same number.
Reducing only one subscript instead of dividing every subscript by the same greatest common factor.
Thinking that the empirical formula always tells the actual number of atoms in a molecule.
For ionic compounds, treating the formula as a discrete molecule instead of a simplest ratio between ions.

explain.body: In order to write down the formula of an ionic compound, first identify the cations and anions and the number of charges present on them. Finally combine the two ions together to form an electrically neutral compound.

explain.title: Use the ion charges
explain.body: Write the symbol of the cation with its charge, then the symbol of the anion with its charge. The charges tell you how many of each ion are needed for a neutral compound.

explain.title: Apply the crisscross method
explain.body: In this method, the numerical value of each of the ion charges is crossed over to become the subscript of the other ion. Signs of the charges are then dropped.

explain.title: Empirical formula
explain.body: Your textbook explains: “To calculate the empirical formula of a compound, you need to determine the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in the compound.” It is the simplest ratio, not necessarily the actual number of atoms in a molecule.

explain.title: Molecular formula
explain.body: Your textbook states: “Molecular formula of a compound can be found out if we know its empirical formula.” The molecular formula gives the actual number of each type of atom in a molecule.

explain.title: Calculate the multiplier
explain.body: Your textbook gives the relationship: “Molecular formula = n (Empirical Formula)” and “Where n = Molar Mass / Empirical Formula mass”. Calculate n, then multiply every subscript by it. If n is one, the molecular and empirical formulas are the same.

explain.title: What a chemical equation represents
explain.body: Representing a chemical change in this way is called a chemical equation. It uses element symbols and compound formulas to show the substances reacting and the substances produced.

explain.title: Reactants and products
explain.body: The reacting substances are called as reactants while those being produced are called products. Reactants are written on the left-hand side and products on the right-hand side, with an arrow between them.

explain.title: Why equations are balanced
explain.body: A chemical equation must obey the law of conservation of mass. This means that no atom should be destroyed or produced during a chemical change. The total number and the type of atoms must remain the same during a chemical change.

explain.title: States and direction
explain.body: Physical states are shown as subscripts: solid is (s), liquid is (l), gas is (g), and aqueous is (aq). A single arrow shows the direction of change; ⇌ indicates a reversible reaction.

explain.title: Reversible reactions and precipitates
explain.body: Such reactions are called as reversible reactions and are indicated by (⇌) sign. An insoluble product such as AgCl comes out of an aqueous solution in the form of a precipitate.

mistakes: Writing the names of substances instead of their correct chemical formulas.
Changing subscripts in formulas to balance an equation; use coefficients instead.
Forgetting that the number and type of atoms must match on both sides.
Putting reactants on the right or products on the left.
Confusing (aq), which means aqueous, with (l), which means liquid.
Using a one-way arrow for a reaction described as reversible.

explain.title: A balanced equation is a recipe
explain.body: A balanced chemical equation tells you the relative numbers of moles that react and form. The coefficients are the mole ratio.

explain.title: Keep the equation correct

explain.title: Mass ratios come from mole ratios

explain.title: Formula writing and balancing
explain.body: Write the correct formula for every reactant and product, then balance the equation with coefficients. Do not change the subscripts in a formula when balancing.

explain.title: The mole and Avogadro's number
explain.body: A mole is an amount of substance containing 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Avogadro's number is the number of particles in one mole.

explain.title: Empirical and molecular formulas
explain.body: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms. A molecular formula gives the actual number of each kind of atom in a molecule and is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

explain.title: Mass and percentage composition
explain.body: Use molar mass to convert between mass and moles. To calculate an element's percentage by mass, divide its mass by the total sample mass and multiply by 100.

explain.title: Stoichiometric calculations
explain.body: A balanced equation gives mole ratios. Convert the given quantity to moles, use the ratio, and then convert the answer to the requested mass or number of particles.

mistakes: Changing formula subscripts instead of adding coefficients when balancing an equation.
Using an unbalanced equation to obtain a mole ratio.
Forgetting to convert grams into moles before using the equation coefficients.
Counting molecules when the question asks for atoms; multiply by the atoms in each molecule.
Confusing the mole, which is an amount of substance, with Avogadro's number, which is a number of particles.
Leaving out units or failing to label which element or substance a final value belongs to.

notes.title: Reading chemical formulae
notes.answer: O₃ shows that one molecule of ozone contains three oxygen atoms.
notes.explanation: An element’s formula shows how that element exists: as single atoms or as molecules. A compound’s formula shows the atoms or ions in it and their ratio. For covalent compounds, the molecular formula shows the kinds and numbers of atoms in one molecule. For ionic compounds, the formula unit gives the minimum ratio of the ions.
notes.simple: A chemical formula is a short way to show which atoms or ions are present and how many of each there are.
examples: O₂ is the formula of an element that exists as molecules: one molecule contains two oxygen atoms.
NaCl is the formula unit of an ionic compound: sodium ions and chloride ions are present in a 1:1 ratio.
steps: Check whether the formula represents an element or a compound.
For an elemental molecule, read the subscript as the number of atoms in one molecule.
For a covalent compound, read the subscripts as the numbers of atoms in one molecule.
For an ionic compound, read the formula as the simplest ratio of its ions.
notes.checkQuestion: What does O₃ tell you about one molecule of ozone?
notes.checkAnswer: O₃ is an elemental molecule with three oxygen atoms in each molecule.

notes.title: Empirical Formula
notes.explanation: An empirical formula gives the simplest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound. To get it from a molecular formula, divide all the subscripts by their greatest common factor.
notes.simple: The molecular formula tells how many atoms are actually in a molecule. The empirical formula tells the simplest ratio between those atoms.
examples: Benzene: C₆H₆ simplifies to CH.
Hydrogen peroxide: H₂O₂ simplifies to HO.
steps: Write the molecular formula: C₆H₆.
Find the greatest common factor of the subscripts: 6.
Divide both subscripts by 6: C₆H₆ → CH.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the empirical formula of C₆H₆?
notes.checkAnswer: C₆H₆ and C₂H₂ both have the empirical formula CH.

notes.title: Writing formulas of binary ionic compounds
notes.answer: Use the ion charges as crossed subscripts to write an electrically neutral formula.
notes.explanation: A binary ionic compound is made from two ions: a cation and an anion. Write their symbols and charges, crisscross the charge numbers to become subscripts, and drop the charge signs. The resulting compound must be electrically neutral.
notes.simple: Balance the positive and negative charges by crossing the charge numbers down as subscripts.
examples: Magnesium nitride: Mg²⁺ and N³⁻ give Mg₃N₂.
Aluminium oxide: Al³⁺ and O²⁻ give Al₂O₃.
steps: Write the symbol and charge of the cation, then the symbol and charge of the anion.
Cross the numerical charge values to become the other ion's subscripts.
Drop the charge signs and write the formula.
notes.checkQuestion: What is the formula of barium nitride?

notes.title: Finding a molecular formula
notes.answer: For empirical formula NO₂, the empirical formula mass is 46. Since 92/46 = 2, multiply both subscripts by 2 to get N₂O₄.
notes.explanation: To find a molecular formula, first find the mass of the empirical formula. Divide the compound’s molar mass by that mass to get n. Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n.
notes.simple: The empirical formula is the smallest atom-count ratio. The molecular formula tells the actual number of each type of atom in one molecule.
examples: Empirical formula CH₂O, molar mass 180: empirical formula mass = 30, n = 180/30 = 6, so molecular formula = C₆H₁₂O₆.
Empirical formula CH, molar mass 78: empirical formula mass = 13, n = 78/13 = 6, so molecular formula = C₆H₆.
steps: Find the empirical formula mass.
Calculate n = molar mass / empirical formula mass.
Multiply every subscript in the empirical formula by n.
Write the resulting molecular formula.
notes.checkQuestion: The empirical formula of a compound is NO₂ and its molar mass is 92 g mol⁻¹. What is its molecular formula?

notes.title: Getting a molecular formula from a structural formula
notes.answer: Write the symbol of each element and its atom count as a subscript; do not write a subscript 1.
notes.explanation: Count every atom shown in the structural formula, write each element symbol, and use the atom counts as subscripts. Omit any subscript of 1.
notes.simple: A structural formula shows how atoms are joined. Count each kind of atom to write the molecular formula.
examples: CH₃—C(=O)—O—H contains 2 C, 4 H and 2 O atoms, so its formula is C₂H₄O₂.
CH₃—CH₂—CH₂—OH contains 3 C, 8 H and 1 O atom, so its formula is C₃H₈O.
steps: Write down the structural formula of the compound.
Count the number of atoms of each type in the structural formula.
Write the symbols of all the elements.
Write the total number of atoms of each kind as a subscript.
Remove the subscript 1.

notes.title: Avogadro's Number and the Mole
notes.explanation: Avogadro's number, Nₐ, is 6.022 × 10²³. It tells us how many units—such as atoms or molecules—are in one mole of a substance. A mole is an amount of substance; Avogadro's number is the number of units in that amount.
notes.simple: A mole is a counting amount, like a dozen. Instead of 12 items, one mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ units.
examples: 1 mole of carbon atoms contains 6.022 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
2 moles of water molecules contain 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules.
steps: Identify whether the question asks for atoms, molecules or moles.
Use Nₐ = 6.022 × 10²³ units per mole.
To find units, multiply moles by Nₐ.
To find moles, divide the number of units by Nₐ.
notes.checkQuestion: How many molecules are in one mole of a substance?
notes.checkAnswer: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ units; Avogadro's number is that count.

notes.title: The Mole and Molar Mass
notes.answer: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles. The molar mass of H₂O is 18 g mol⁻¹.
notes.explanation: A mole is a counting unit for particles. One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ particles, and the particles may be atoms, molecules or ions. Molar mass is the mass of one mole of a substance. To find a compound’s molar mass, multiply each element’s atomic mass by its subscript and add the contributions.
notes.simple: A mole is a very large counting unit: like a dozen means 12, a mole means 6.022 × 10²³ particles. Molar mass tells you the mass of that mole.
examples: One mole of O₂ contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules and has a mass of 32 g.
steps: Identify the elements in the formula and their subscripts.
Multiply each atomic mass by the number of atoms of that element.
Add the contributions.
Write the molar mass in g mol⁻¹.

notes.title: Chemical Equations and Reactions
notes.explanation: A chemical equation represents a chemical change using symbols and formulas. It shows the reactants, the products, and how they are related.
notes.simple: A chemical equation is a recipe for a chemical change: it shows what starts the reaction and what is made.
examples: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂
N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃
steps: Write the correct formulas for the reactants and products.
Put the reactants on the left and the products on the right, with an arrow between them.
Balance the equation so each type of atom occurs equally on both sides.
Show physical states when known: (s), (l), (g), or (aq).
Use ⇌ when the reaction can proceed in both directions.
notes.checkQuestion: In a chemical equation, which side shows the products?
notes.checkAnswer: Reactants are on the left; products are on the right. The equation must have the same number and type of atoms on both sides.

notes.title: Calculations from a chemical equation
notes.answer: A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratio between reactants and products. This ratio can be used to calculate how much of a substance reacts or is produced.
notes.explanation: A balanced chemical equation gives the mole ratio between reactants and products. Use that ratio to work out the amount of a substance that reacts or forms, then convert between moles and mass or particles if needed.
notes.simple: The numbers in a balanced equation act like a recipe. They show how much of each substance reacts and how much product is made.
examples: In CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂, 100 g of CaCO₃ produces 111 g of CaCl₂.
In 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O, 4 g of H₂ produces 36 g of H₂O.
steps: Write the balanced chemical equation.
Use its coefficients to find the mole ratio, or use the molar masses to find the mass ratio.

notes.title: Stoichiometry: counting particles and calculating amounts
notes.explanation: Stoichiometry uses a balanced chemical equation and mole ratios to calculate amounts of reactants and products. Convert the given amount to moles, use the equation, then convert to the required unit.
notes.simple: A balanced equation is like a recipe: its numbers tell you the mole ratios. Convert what you are given into moles, follow the ratio, and convert to the requested amount.
examples: For 10 g of CH₄: 10 ÷ 16 = 0.625 mol CH₄.

How much SO₂ is needed in grams to produce 10 moles of sulphur?

2H₂S(g) + SO₂(g) → 2H₂O(l) + 3S(s)
modelAnswer: From the equation, 1 mol SO₂ produces 3 mol S.
Moles of SO₂ needed = 10 mol S × (1 mol SO₂ ÷ 3 mol S) = 10/3 mol.
Molar mass of SO₂ = 32 + 2(16) = 64 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of SO₂ = (10/3 mol) × 64 g mol⁻¹ = 213.3 g.
Answer: 213.3 g SO₂.

How much ammonia is needed in grams to produce 1 kg of urea fertilizer?

2NH₃(aq) + CO₂(aq) → CO(NH₂)₂(aq) + H₂O(l)
modelAnswer: Given: mass of urea = 1 kg = 1000 g.
Molar mass of CO(NH₂)₂ = 12 + 16 + 2(14) + 4(1) = 60 g mol⁻¹.
Moles of urea = 1000 g ÷ 60 g mol⁻¹ = 16.667 mol.
From the equation, NH₃ : urea = 2 : 1.
Moles of NH₃ needed = 2 × 16.667 = 33.333 mol.
Molar mass of NH₃ = 14 + 3(1) = 17 g mol⁻¹.
Mass of NH₃ = 33.333 mol × 17 g mol⁻¹ = 566.7 g NH₃.
